title: Enquiry opened
body:
At 08:40 this morning the editor reported the Communal Tin missing. The tin, which is round, tartan and full of Assorted Shortbread, was posted to him by Head Office in February with the instruction “to be shared with the team”. The team is spread across three countries, so the editor put it somewhere very safe while he designed a Sharing Framework. The Framework is now on draft four. The tin is at large.

An enquiry has been opened. The editor has appointed himself Senior Investigating Officer after a rigorous process in which he was the only applicant, the interview panel and, briefly, the person who made the coffee. His first act was to buy a notebook. His second was to write ENQUIRY on the front in capitals and underline it twice. Asked when the tin was last seen, he consulted the notebook, found it empty and said the investigation was “at an early stage”.
theory: Probably the cat.

title: The incident room
body:
The enquiry now has an incident room. It used to be the spare room, and before that it was the room where the exercise bike went to be forgotten. The editor has pinned a map of the world to the wall and linked the UK, Cebu and Sydney with red string. This took ninety minutes and established that the three desks are a long way apart, which the enquiry already knew, because that is why the tin was never shared.

A suspect board has gone up beside the map. So far it holds a photograph of the cat and a sticky note that says “THE CEILING?”, because the editor remembered that a reindeer in this paper pointed upwards. Asked what evidence he had against the ceiling, the editor said that was exactly the kind of question a ceiling would want asked.
theory: The cat, possibly working with the ceiling.

title: The reindeer is questioned
body:
Following today’s front page, the editor interviewed the reindeer seen in reception. The interview took place over video. The reindeer joined on time, with his camera on and a tidy professional background, which the editor found suspicious in itself.

The editor asked him to account for his movements in March. The reindeer said he had been busy in March but wouldn’t say with what. The editor suggested Christmas preparations. The reindeer said “in March?” in a way the editor found rude.

The interview ended when the editor’s screen froze mid-sentence, with his mouth open and one finger raised. The reindeer said afterwards that the picture had been “oddly well framed, like the camera was sitting on a box or something”. The editor took this as a compliment and wrote it down under Compliments.
theory: The reindeer is the brains. The cat is the muscle. The ceiling is the getaway.

title: A search of the museum
body:
Acting on a hunch, the editor searched the museum in the spare room, reasoning that a thief might hide a stolen tin among other exhibits. The museum has one exhibit, the mug. The tin was not in the mug, under the mug or behind the label that says Dishwasher Safe.

On his hands and knees under the display table, the editor found two things: the remote control that went missing in 2023, and a single shortbread crumb. He sealed the crumb in a sandwich bag labelled EXHIBIT B. Then, overcome by the importance of the moment, he sneezed it out of the bag.

The editor has asked us not to record the sneeze. It has been recorded.
theory: Someone has been eating shortbread in the museum. The cat cannot open tins. Or can it?

title: A fingertip search
body:
The weekend gave the enquiry time for a full fingertip search of the house. It turned up three remote controls, a charger for a phone the editor no longer owns, eleven pens (none of which work) and a birthday card he was meant to post in October. It did not turn up the tin.

The search did not include the desk. The editor explained that the desk is “where the work happens”. Searching your own desk, he said, is what people do when they have lost something, and he has not lost anything because the tin was stolen. He then spent four minutes looking for his glasses, which were on his head. He has asked us not to record that either.
theory: Stolen to order. Possibly an international operation.

title: The only witness
body:
A breakthrough. At the back of the kitchen drawer, behind the takeaway menus, the editor found a single shortbread finger. It had been separated from the rest of the tin in February and has been living quietly there ever since.

The witness was brought to the incident room and put on a saucer for questioning. It said nothing, which the editor took to be fear. He asked it gently where the others were. It said nothing. He leaned in close and whispered, “Just point.” The shortbread finger, lying exactly where he had put it, pointed directly at the laptop.

The editor thanked the witness for its time, noted that it was clearly confused, and ate it. Asked later whether it had been wise to eat the only witness, he said it was “a judgement call” and “very nice, actually, a bit soft”.
theory: The witness was protecting someone.

title: A compliment is investigated
body:
During a call this week, a colleague told the editor he had looked “really professional on camera lately” and asked whether he had a new set-up. The editor has been waiting since March for someone to say this. He thanked them at length and explained his approach to ergonomics, which he called “holistic”. The call overran by eleven minutes.

Only afterwards did it occur to the editor that the comment might be evidence. He wrote it down under “Lately”, which he defined as “since about March”. Then he wrote “March” again, circled it and drew an arrow to the cat.
theory: The cat, in March.

title: Exhibit A is measured
body:
Today’s front page reports a circular mark on the editor’s desk. The enquiry has measured it with a borrowed tape measure, and it is nineteen centimetres across. The tin, according to the manufacturer’s website, which the editor read three times, is also nineteen centimetres across.

The editor called this “a very interesting coincidence” and wrote it down. Then he noticed that the mark is exactly where the laptop sat before March, and wrote that down too, on a separate page, so the two facts wouldn’t get muddled up.

He has ordered tests on the mark. The tests involve licking a finger, touching the mark and saying “hmm”. Results are expected in the new year.
theory: The tin was on the desk and somebody took it off the desk. Find out who uses this desk.

title: Surveillance
body:
Inspired by today’s picture desk, the editor has put the garden under surveillance, convinced that the robin on the fork is a lookout. He watched it from the kitchen window for six hours and took notes. The robin ate a worm, looked at the editor and left.

A neighbour reports that their doorbell camera caught the editor at 14:20 holding up a sign to the robin that read “WE KNOW”. The robin did not respond. The neighbour has asked whether everything is all right at home. The editor assured them it is “an active enquiry”.
theory: A ring of garden birds. The robin is the lookout; the brains are elsewhere.

title: The bait
body:
Today the enquiry tried to lure the tin home by baking a batch of shortbread and leaving it by the back door, on the theory that tins, like cats, come back to familiar smells. The shortbread burned. The smoke alarm went off during a call with a client, who asked whether everything was all right and then, kindly, whether the editor had “got a new chair”, because he was “sitting very tall today”.

The editor said he has always been tall. He has not always been tall. Everyone who has met him in person agrees that he is average.
theory: The tin has gone to ground. It may have left the country inside a chimney.

title: The Working Group
body:
The enquiry has set up a Working Group. Its only member is the editor. He has also produced a RACI chart, in which he is Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed, and Terms of Reference that thank him for agreeing to take part.

The first meeting lasted an hour. The minutes, taken by the editor, record that the editor raised a point, the editor disagreed, and the editor agreed to take it offline. Under Any Other Business, the editor asked whether anyone else could hear a faint rattle when he typed. Nobody else could. Nobody else was there.
theory: Someone with access to the house, a motive involving shortbread and an unusual amount of time on their hands.

title: A police sketch
body:
With a weekend to fill, the editor has drawn a sketch of the suspect from the descriptions gathered so far: tall on camera but not in person, at the desk a great deal, often near the laptop, fond of shortbread, and active since March.

The sketch shows a middle-aged man in a fleece, sitting at a laptop and looking pleased with his posture. The editor has pinned it to the board and called it “a very typical face”. He has asked readers to look out for this man. Several have written in to say they see him every day.
theory: A typical man. Possibly local. Owns a fleece.

title: The houseplant is cleared
body:
Today’s gardening column reports that the houseplant has done well since being moved six inches to the left. The enquiry asks: moved by whom, why, and to make room for what?

The plant was questioned for forty minutes and made no statement. Its soil was searched and contained no crumbs. The editor apologised to the plant, watered it as a gesture of goodwill, then overwatered it out of guilt. The plant is cleared of all suspicion and is recovering on a saucer. It is the second thing this month to be put on that saucer for questioning, and the first to survive.
theory: A plant could not have done this. Something taller.

title: An anonymous letter
body:
The enquiry has received its first anonymous letter. It reads, in full: “Have you tried looking under things?”

The editor called this “a gift” and spent the afternoon looking under things. He looked under the sofa, the rug, the bed, the doormat and the cat. He climbed into the loft to look under the ceiling from above, which is technically looking at the floor, and stayed there for some time after the ladder fell over.

He did not look under the laptop. Asked why not, he said “a laptop isn’t a thing, it’s a tool”, and that whoever wrote the letter had “clearly never worked in operations”.
theory: Whoever wrote the letter knows more than they’re saying. Possibly the ceiling.

title: The smart speaker gives evidence
body:
Today’s front page mentions a witness who heard a sound “broadly consistent with a custard cream”. We can now reveal that the witness is the smart speaker in the kitchen. It overheard a rattle from the study and, when the editor asked it to “play back what you heard”, played a podcast about sourdough.

Under further questioning, the speaker confirmed that it hears the rattle every time someone types an angry email. The editor asked how often that is. The speaker said, “Forty-one times this week.” The editor asked it to stop being dramatic. The speaker said, “Okay, playing Dramatic Music”, and did so for the rest of the afternoon, because nobody could remember how to make it stop.
theory: The rattle is a coded message.

title: Interrogation music
body:
To unsettle the suspects, the editor asked Enviro FM to play “interrogation music” on a loop in the incident room. The request line suggested something with a strong bass. Within minutes the laptop began buzzing gently against whatever it was standing on, in time with the music, like a small metal drum.

The editor danced to it. He has asked us not to describe the dancing, and in fairness, we couldn’t.
theory: The suspects are rattled. Something in this room is literally rattled.

title: Payroll replies
body:
The reindeer has returned with a reference from Payroll (see front page) and is released without charge. The editor then turned his attention to Payroll, emailing to ask whether they had noticed “any unexplained shortbread” in this year’s figures.

Payroll replied within the hour. They had not noticed any shortbread. They had, however, noticed an expense claim from the editor dated 5 March for “one ergonomic laptop riser, tartan”, at a cost of £0.00, with the note “found it in the house, bargain”. They asked why it had been submitted at all. The editor replied that he “believes in transparency”. Payroll replied that they believe in fewer emails.
theory: Payroll know something.

title: Customs
body:
International post has landed, and the editor met it at the border, convinced the tin had been smuggled out in a parcel. Customs let him look through the scanner logs, on condition that he stopped asking about the pun they’re holding.

The logs were clean. No tin has crossed any border this year. Customs did add one note, which the editor read aloud before he had properly understood it: “The only tartan item to appear on any of our screens this year is visible on the editor’s own video calls, just below his laptop, at the bottom of the picture.” He has since moved his laptop, and himself, out of shot.
theory: An international smuggling ring, tartan division.

title: Corrections
body:
The enquiry wishes to correct the following. The cat mentioned on 1, 2 and 4 December is a cushion. The editor does not own a cat. He owns a cat-shaped cushion, a gift from a relative, and he has been questioning it all month. The ceiling has asked to be taken off the suspect board, and we are happy to confirm it played no part. The reindeer did nothing wrong. Payroll did nothing wrong. The robin did nothing wrong, although it did look at us in a certain way.

Finally, the team email the editor sent on 6 March, “Exciting news re: my home office”, included a photograph captioned “my new tartan stand — game changer”. We regret that the enquiry did not read it at the time. Neither, it now turns out, did anyone else.
theory: Back to square one, which, the editor points out, is not the shape of the tin.

title: The crossword
body:
In a last attempt to draw out a confession, the editor set a crossword for all the remaining suspects. The answers were TIN, UNDER, LAPTOP, TARTAN, MARCH and YOU. He left it on the desk overnight in case anyone felt guilty enough to fill it in.

In the morning it had been completed, in his own handwriting. He is now considering whether the culprit has been forging his handwriting, which he calls “the obvious explanation”.
theory: Forgery.

title: The handover
body:
Exhausted, the editor handed the enquiry to the Cebu and Sydney desks for the night, along with forty pages of notes, the map, the string and the instruction “don’t touch anything”.

Cebu solved the case in four minutes. Sydney checked the answer in two more and added a smiley face. They left a single sticky note on the handover for the editor to find in the morning: “Lift the laptop.”

The editor read it, nodded and said it was “a great motto”. He has had it printed on a mug. The mug is on the desk now, next to the laptop, which he has not lifted.
theory: The overseas desks are toying with me.

title: The findings deck
body:
With the enquiry due to report, the editor presented his findings on an all-staff call. He had prepared forty-seven slides. Slide one said “WHO?”. Slides two to forty-six were stock photos of biscuits. Slide forty-seven said “Questions?”, and there were several, mostly about why he looked so tall.

An independent witness (see front page) then asked him to tilt his camera down to show his desk. What happened next is on the front page. The enquiry’s own notes record only “tartan??”, in very small writing.
theory: Someone tall. Someone close. Someone with presence.

title: The verdict approaches
body:
The editor has announced that he will name the culprit tomorrow. He has narrowed it down to the cushion, the ceiling, Payroll, the robin, or “a person unknown, probably tall, probably in a fleece, possibly at this very desk”.

He spent the evening packing for the Christmas break and left his packing list on the desk. It reads: 1. Charger. 2. Notebook (ENQUIRY). 3. Laptop. 4. Find out why laptop is so heavy. 5. Lift the laptop (mug).
theory: Tomorrow. Everything tomorrow.

title: Findings of the enquiry
body:
The enquiry presents its findings. The Communal Tin was never stolen. On 4 March it was placed under the editor’s laptop as an “ergonomic riser”, claimed on expenses at £0.00, photographed for a team email and then forgotten. For nine months the editor appeared noticeably taller on every call and accepted every compliment.

The enquiry finds the editor Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed. He is sentenced to share the shortbread with colleagues in three countries, as originally instructed. He proposed a Sharing Framework, and it was rejected. The shortbread will instead be divided equally among everyone who reads this paper, which by the enquiry’s calculations comes to roughly one crumb each. Delivery arrangements are under review by the Working Group, which is him.

The cushion, the ceiling, the reindeer, the robin, the houseplant, Payroll and the smart speaker are owed an apology and have received one. The shortbread finger is owed an apology and cannot receive one. The case is closed. The laptop now rests on a stack of paperbacks, and the editor is, once again, average.
theory: Case closed. It was me.
